title: Docstring falsely claims the return value is a JWT
why: Callers and reviewers reading the docstring will assume the token is a standards-compliant JWT (three base64url segments, verifiable with any JWT library). In reality the function returns a two-part string `sha1hex.user_id` — not a JWT. Code that tries to decode or verify it as a JWT will fail silently or with a misleading error.
evidence:
"""Returns a signed JWT valid for 24 hours."""
return hashlib.sha1(raw.encode()).hexdigest() + "." + str(user_id)
fix:
"""Returns a token of the form ``<sha1hex>.<user_id>``.

The sha1 is computed over ``user_id + '|' + unix_timestamp + '|' + JWT_SECRET``.
Note: expiry is embedded in the token but is NOT verified by ``current_user_id()``;
callers should not rely on the token expiring automatically.
"""

title: Docstring claims tokens expire after 24 hours — expiry is never enforced
why: A caller reading 'valid for 24 hours' will assume that old tokens are automatically rejected. However, `current_user_id()` never inspects the timestamp embedded in the token — it extracts the user_id from the second dot-segment without any validation. Tokens are therefore valid indefinitely, making any revocation or session-lifetime reasoning based on the docstring incorrect.
fix: Add to the `issue_token` docstring: 'The timestamp is embedded in the token but expiry is not enforced by `current_user_id()`; tokens do not expire.' Also update or remove the '24 hours' claim entirely until expiry checking is implemented.

title: No docstring — callers cannot tell what the function accepts or returns
why: The function is the sole identity mechanism used by three routes (`search`, `create_note`, `filter_notes`). Without a docstring, a caller does not know: (a) what format `token` must have, (b) that it returns `None` rather than raising on a missing/malformed token, or (c) that the user_id is taken from the token's second segment with no signature verification — meaning any string of the form `<anything>.<integer>` is accepted as a valid identity.
fix:
"""Extract the user ID from a token produced by ``issue_token``.

Args:
    token: A string of the form ``<sha1hex>.<user_id>``, typically passed as
           the value of the ``Authorization`` request header.

Returns:
    The integer user ID, or ``None`` if ``token`` is falsy or not in the
    expected two-part format.

Warning:
    The signature (sha1 prefix) is **not verified**. Any string matching
    ``<anything>.<integer>`` will be accepted and its integer part returned.
    Expiry is also not checked.
"""

title: No docstring — callers cannot tell what header is checked or where the secret comes from
why: The function is the only authorization gate for the DELETE endpoint. Without a docstring, reviewers do not know: (a) which header is inspected (`X-Admin-Token`), (b) that the comparison is against the `ADMIN_BYPASS_TOKEN` config value (a hardcoded string `letmein-admin`), or (c) that there is no rate-limiting, HMAC, or cryptographic protection — a bare string equality check.
fix:
"""Return True if the request carries a valid admin token.

Checks the ``X-Admin-Token`` header against the ``ADMIN_BYPASS_TOKEN``
configuration value using a plain string comparison (no HMAC / timing-safe
check). Returns ``False`` for any absent or non-matching value.

Args:
    request_headers: A Flask/Werkzeug headers object (or any mapping)
                     providing ``.get()``.

Returns:
    bool
"""

title: No docstring — dangerous `eval` on caller-supplied input is completely undocumented
why: The function runs `eval(expression)` where `expression` is a string submitted directly by the end-user via the `POST /notes/filter` body. The absence of any docstring means neither the route author nor future maintainers will notice the code-execution risk from reading the signature alone. A caller who documents their own code based on this function's apparent contract ('it filters notes') will not realise they are exposing arbitrary Python execution to every authenticated user.
evidence:
def applyFilterExpression(notes, expression):
    return [n for n in notes if eval(expression)]
fix:
"""Filter ``notes`` by evaluating ``expression`` against each row.

**Security warning:** ``expression`` is passed directly to ``eval()`` with no
sandboxing. This allows arbitrary Python code execution. Do **not** use this
function with untrusted (user-supplied) input until a safe expression evaluator
replaces ``eval``.

Args:
    notes: Iterable of note rows (tuples of ``(id, title, body)``).
    expression: A Python expression string. The variable ``n`` is bound to the
                current note row inside the eval context.

Returns:
    A list of note rows for which ``expression`` evaluated to a truthy value.

Raises:
    Any exception raised by ``eval`` propagates to the caller.
"""

title: No docstring — silent error suppression is invisible to callers
why: The function catches all exceptions with a bare `except: pass`, meaning that a failed DELETE (e.g. a database constraint violation, connection error, or a note that does not exist) returns `None` without any indication of failure. The calling route `remove_note` always responds `204 No Content`, giving the admin no way to tell whether the deletion actually succeeded. This behaviour is completely hidden from callers who have no docstring to read.
fix:
"""Delete the note with the given ``note_id`` from the database.

Args:
    note_id: Integer primary key of the note to delete.

Returns:
    None in all cases.

Warning:
    All database exceptions are silently swallowed (``except: pass``). A
    missing note or a DB error will not raise; callers receive no signal
    that the deletion failed.
"""

title: No docstring on DELETE route — authorization requirement undocumented
why: The route silently returns 403 for non-admin callers, but there is no docstring describing the expected `X-Admin-Token` header, the 204 success response, or the fact that deletion failures are swallowed by `delete_note`. Developers wiring up clients or writing API documentation have no inline guidance.
fix:
"""DELETE /notes/<note_id> — remove a note (admin only).

Requires the ``X-Admin-Token`` header to match the configured admin bypass
token. Returns 403 if the header is absent or incorrect.

Returns 204 No Content on success. Note: deletion failures inside
``delete_note`` are silently suppressed; a 204 does not guarantee the row
was actually removed.
"""

title: No docstring on filter route — eval risk and full traceback leak undocumented
why: The route passes the user-supplied `expression` field to `applyFilterExpression`, which calls `eval`. The error handler exposes the full Python traceback in the JSON response. Neither fact is visible from the route definition alone. Developers reading just the route signature will not know the endpoint executes arbitrary code or that internal stack traces are leaked to the caller.
fix:
"""POST /notes/filter — return the authenticated user's notes matching a filter expression.

Request body (JSON):
    expression (str): A Python expression evaluated against each note row via
                      ``eval()``. The variable ``n`` is the current row tuple.

**Security warning:** ``expression`` is executed with ``eval()`` — arbitrary
code execution is possible. This endpoint must not be exposed to untrusted users
until the evaluator is sandboxed.

On error, returns a 500 response containing the exception message **and the
full Python traceback**, which may leak internal implementation details.
"""
